sections.title: Reading Passage — The NFPA 704 Hazard Diamond
body: Before you touch any chemical in the lab, you should be able to read its hazard information. One of the most important tools is the NFPA 704 hazard diamond — sometimes called a 'fire diamond' — developed by the National Fire Protection Agency. It summarizes the major hazards of a chemical substance in a single symbol.

The diamond is divided into four colored sections. The top (red) diamond specifies the level of fire hazard, based on the temperature range for the substance's flash point. The blue (left) diamond indicates the level of health hazard. The yellow (right) diamond describes reactivity hazards — how readily the substance will undergo detonation or a violent chemical change. The white (bottom) diamond points out special hazards, such as whether the substance is an oxidizer, reacts dangerously with water, is corrosive, or is radioactive.

Each hazard is rated on a scale from 0 to 4: 0 means no hazard and 4 means extremely hazardous. A chemical rated 4 for health, for example, is deadly even with brief exposure — while a rating of 1 means only mild irritation. Reading these numbers tells you exactly how careful you need to be.

The hazards the diamond describes are chemical properties — characteristics of a substance that describe its ability to change into different matter. Flammability, toxicity, and reactivity are all chemical properties. Physical properties like density, color, and melting point describe a substance without changing its composition. Knowing the difference helps you predict how a chemical will behave before you use it.
common_mistakes: Memorizing the diamond colors without the meaning — red is fire, blue is health, yellow is reactivity, white is special.
Confusing 'physical property' with 'chemical property' — flammability is chemical (it involves burning, a chemical change); melting point is physical.

sections.title: The NFPA 704 Hazard Diamond
sections.caption: Figure 1. The NFPA 704 hazard diamond: red (top) = fire hazard, blue (left) = health hazard, yellow (right) = reactivity, white (bottom) = special hazards. Each is rated 0 (no hazard) to 4 (extreme hazard).

items.q: Which section of the NFPA 704 diamond indicates the level of fire hazard?
items.explain: The top, red diamond specifies fire hazard based on the flash point temperature range.

items.q: The blue (left) section of the hazard diamond indicates:
items.explain: The blue diamond on the left indicates the level of health hazard of the substance.

items.q: The yellow (right) section of the hazard diamond describes:
choices: How readily the substance detonates or undergoes violent chemical change
items.answer: How readily the substance detonates or undergoes violent chemical change
items.explain: Yellow (right) = reactivity hazards, such as detonation or violent chemical change.

items.q: A rating of 4 in any section of the hazard diamond means the hazard level is:
items.explain: Each hazard is rated 0 (no hazard) to 4 (extremely hazardous).

items.q: Which special hazard would appear in the white (bottom) section of the diamond?
items.explain: The white (bottom) diamond points out special hazards: oxidizer, reacts dangerously with water, corrosive, radioactive, etc.

items.q: A chemical is rated 0 for fire hazard. This means it:
choices: Has a very low flash point
items.explain: 0 = no hazard: a fire rating of 0 means the substance will not burn.

items.q: Flammability is described by the diamond as a:
items.explain: Flammability is a chemical property (burning changes the substance's composition) and is rated in the red fire-hazard section.

items.q: Which two hazards would you MOST expect to see rated high for nitroglycerin?
items.explain: The textbook notes nitroglycerin is very dangerous because it explodes easily — high fire AND reactivity ratings.

sections.title: Part B — Physical vs Chemical Properties (Questions 9–14)

items.q: Classify: 'Iron combines with oxygen in the presence of water to form rust.'
items.explain: Rusting changes iron into a different substance (iron oxide) — a chemical property of iron.

items.q: Classify: 'The melting point of iron is 1538 °C.'
items.explain: Melting point is observed without changing the chemical composition — a physical property.

items.q: Classify: 'Neon poses almost no hazard because it is very unreactive.'
items.explain: Reactivity describes the ability to undergo chemical change — a chemical property. Neon's unreactivity is why it is safe.

items.q: Which of the following is a CHEMICAL change?
items.explain: Rusting produces a new substance (iron oxide). Melting, dissolving, and condensing change state/form without changing composition.

items.q: Which of the following is a PHYSICAL change?
items.explain: Grinding changes the form of the substance but not its chemical composition — a physical change.

items.q: Classify: 'A drop of hot cooking oil causes brief discomfort, but a pot of hot oil yields severe burns.' The temperature is the same — this is because temperature is:
items.explain: Temperature is intensive — the same in a drop or a pot. The pot has more HEAT, which is extensive (depends on amount).

items.q: Classify: 'The mass of the sample is 45.8 kg.'
items.explain: Mass depends on the amount of matter — an extensive property.

items.q: Classify: 'The density of aluminum is 2.70 g/cm³.'
items.explain: Density does not depend on the amount of the sample — a small piece and a large block have the same density.

items.q: Classify: 'The volume of the solution is 250 mL.'
items.explain: Volume depends on the amount of matter — an extensive property.

sections.title: GHS Hazard Symbols
sections.caption: Figure 2. GHS hazard pictograms used on chemical labels. While the NFPA diamond rates hazards 0-4 in the lab, GHS pictograms communicate hazards on labels with standardized symbols.

sections.title: Part D — GHS Pictograms & The Diamond (Questions 18–22)

items.q: A container's label shows the GHS flame pictogram. This warns that the substance is:
items.explain: The flame pictogram warns the substance catches fire easily.

items.q: The GHS skull-and-crossbones pictogram means the substance is:
choices: Acutely toxic — can be fatal if swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed
items.answer: Acutely toxic — can be fatal if swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed
items.explain: The skull and crossbones is the GHS acute toxicity pictogram.

items.q: Which GHS pictogram appears on a container of a substance that intensifies fires?
items.explain: The flame-over-circle pictogram means the substance is an oxidizer — it intensifies fires.

items.q: The NFPA diamond is MOST commonly found:
items.explain: The hazard diamond appears on chemical containers in labs and workplaces to summarize hazards at a glance.

items.q: A substance is rated 4 for reactivity in its hazard diamond. Before using it you should:
choices: Handle it normally — ratings are just suggestions
Follow special precautions; it may detonate or react violently
Assume it is safe because it has a label
Only avoid touching it with bare hands
items.answer: Follow special precautions; it may detonate or react violently
items.explain: 4 = extremely hazardous reactivity: the substance may detonate or undergo violent chemical change — special precautions required.

items.q: Which glassware is BEST for measuring an exact liquid volume?
items.explain: Graduated cylinders have precise volume markings; beakers and flasks are for holding and mixing.

items.q: Which piece of equipment provides controlled flame heat?
items.explain: The Bunsen burner mixes gas with air to produce a controllable flame.

items.q: Which item protects your eyes from chemical splashes?
items.explain: Goggles form a seal around the eyes; safety glasses do not. Goggles are required for chemical work.

items.q: A pipette is used to:
choices: Measure and transfer small volumes of liquid precisely
items.answer: Measure and transfer small volumes of liquid precisely
items.explain: Pipettes transfer small, precise liquid volumes — essential for accurate lab work.

items.q: The Erlenmeyer flask's narrow neck and wide base are useful because they:
items.explain: The narrow neck keeps liquid inside while swirling — ideal for mixing and titrations.

items.q: What should you do FIRST if a chemical splashes into your eye?
choices: Rub the eye to remove the chemical
Flush the eye with water for at least 15 minutes and tell the teacher
Wait to see if it hurts
Put on goggles after the fact
items.answer: Flush the eye with water for at least 15 minutes and tell the teacher
items.explain: Immediate, prolonged flushing dilutes and removes the chemical. Rubbing spreads it and causes more damage.

items.q: Explain how the four sections of the NFPA 704 hazard diamond work together to keep you safe.
items.answer: The diamond summarizes four hazards in one symbol: fire (top red, from flash point), health (left blue), reactivity (right yellow, detonation/violent change), and special hazards (bottom white, e.g. oxidizer, reacts with water). Each is rated 0-4. Reading it before handling a chemical tells you the level of each hazard so you can take appropriate precautions.
items.explain: One glance at the diamond communicates four independent hazard ratings.

items.q: Why is flammability classified as a chemical property rather than a physical property?
items.answer: Flammability describes the ability of a substance to undergo combustion — a chemical change that produces new substances (carbon dioxide and water). Physical properties are observed without changing the chemical composition. Since burning always changes the substance into new matter, flammability is a chemical property.
items.explain: Chemical properties describe how a substance changes into different matter; flammability, toxicity, and reactivity all fit this definition.

items.q: A lab container shows a hazard diamond rated 2-3-1 with an oxidizer symbol in the white section. Describe what each number means and how you would handle the substance.
items.answer: The ratings are fire (top) 2, health (left) 3, reactivity (right) 1: moderate fire hazard, high health hazard, low reactivity, plus special hazard = oxidizer (intensifies fires). Handling: wear full PPE (goggles, gloves, lab coat), avoid skin contact and inhalation (health 3), keep away from flammable materials (oxidizer + fire 2), and follow the teacher's specific precautions.
items.explain: Reading each quadrant independently and acting on the highest ratings is the point of the diamond.

sections.title: Key Terms
items: NFPA 704
Hazard identification system using a diamond with fire, health, reactivity, and special hazard ratings
hazard diamond
Symbol that summarizes the major hazards of a chemical substance (0 = no hazard, 4 = extremely hazardous)
flash point
Lowest temperature at which vapors ignite — basis of the fire hazard rating
physical property
Characteristic observed without changing chemical composition (density, color, melting point)
chemical property
Characteristic describing ability to change into different matter (flammability, toxicity, reactivity)
physical change
Change in state or form without changing chemical composition (melting, dissolving, grinding)
chemical change
Change that produces new substances (rusting, burning, rotting)
extensive property
Depends on the amount of matter (mass, volume, heat)
intensive property
Does not depend on the amount of matter (density, temperature, color)
GHS
Globally Harmonized System — standardized hazard pictograms on chemical labels
oxidizer
Substance that intensifies fires (special hazard symbol)
